strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk: repeated target stimuli across subjects can let powerful language decoders memorize test text and substantially inflate apparent brain-to-text performance.

The experiments cover two signal modalities, two datasets, two established models, and several splitting strategies. Additional held-out tests, shuffled-signal controls, and teacher-forcing ablations provide qualitatively convergent evidence that some commonly used evaluations measure decoder memorization more than neural decoding.
Separating subject overlap from stimulus overlap is useful, and a benchmark holding out both dimensions would be valuable for evaluating joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen language.
The topic is directly relevant to NLP, and the main intuition is communicated clearly through the graphical split taxonomy.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. Subject-held-out/seen-stimulus, seen-subject/unseen-stimulus, and jointly held-out evaluation measure different generalization regimes. Sharing stimuli is not automatically data leakage if the intended estimand is transfer to a new subject on a fixed stimulus set. The paper does not justify why joint subject-and-stimulus generalization is the uniquely correct definition of cross-subject decoding, so claims that all prior splits are wrong or meaningless do not follow.

The formal definitions and leakage metrics are not sound as written. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification where existence of any overlap appears intended. Equations 17–20 refer to intersections of nominally disjoint train/test sample sets and do not correctly encode sharing a subject or text label. Consequently, values such as a roughly 12.5% BSLR for splits in which every test subject is represented in training are difficult to interpret as leakage rates.

The proposed algorithms are inconsistent with the stated criterion. Equations 13–14 require both subject and stimulus membership in the same partition, whereas Algorithm 1's expansion checks only subject membership and Algorithm 2 checks only story membership; these procedures can reintroduce the very overlap they are meant to prevent. The pseudocode also contains dimension/indexing inconsistencies, and the greedy fMRI construction is not proven to yield disjoint subject sets. The proof that samples must always be discarded is false without additional assumptions on the incidence graph.

The clean split discards an unspecified amount of data, but the paper reports neither retained sample/subject/story counts nor realized split ratios. Comparisons therefore confound leakage with training-set size, test-set size, story difficulty, and simultaneous distribution shifts. No optimality analysis supports the claim that the construction discards as little data as possible.

Several central empirical interpretations are invalid or weakly supported. Decreasing validation loss does not itself demonstrate overfitting or degrading representations, and continued test improvement with more training is not diagnostic of leakage. The longer-training comparison also changes learning rate and encoder initialization, while the predicted encoder pattern fails on EEG.

Results are insufficiently reproducible: no code, concrete split assignments, output examples, training seeds, uncertainty estimates, significance tests, metric implementation details, or adequate description of the additional test-set construction are provided. Only the leakage-rate calculation is repeated across seeds.

There are troubling internal inconsistencies. Appendix E describes methods (d) and (e) as having no text leakage although the main tables classify them as leaking; Table 8's method-(d) results conflict sharply with the main results; and some reported ROUGE precision, recall, and F values are mutually inconsistent. The advertised fair benchmark also reproduces the teacher-forced scores even though free generation is the appropriate decoding evaluation.

The audit covers only two models and two datasets and does not establish the sweeping claim about all current cross-subject methods. The promising core observation remains salvageable, but the split definition, algorithm, reporting, and causal experiments require substantial correction and rerunning before the contribution is sound and reproducible.

strengths: The manuscript identifies an important evaluation risk in brain-to-text research: repeated target text can let a strong decoder score well without using the brain signal. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-tt6wpzj8/call-89168af7311b49a3bd63ad0cdb8b6dd2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The additional-test-set, shuffled-input, longer-training, and teacher-forcing analyses attack the central concern from several directions. In particular, the small effect of shuffling under text-overlapping splits is compelling evidence that reported scores can largely reflect target memorization.
The subject–stimulus graph formulation usefully exposes two distinct generalization axes, and experiments span fMRI and EEG, two public datasets, and two established architectures.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and candid that its stricter split discards observations and does not improve model architecture.
weaknesses: The paper does not justify its central normative claim that every split with subject or stimulus overlap is “wrong” or constitutes data leakage. Subject-held-out, stimulus-held-out, and jointly held-out evaluation answer different scientific questions; repeated stimuli across independent subjects can be intentional when isolating cross-subject generalization. The proposed protocol should be framed as joint subject-and-stimulus generalization, not as the uniquely correct cross-subject split.

Several formal definitions are incorrect as written. Equations 6–7 use a universal condition over training samples where leakage requires an existential overlap, while Equations 17–20 count intersections of training and test graphs that should be empty for ordinary sample-disjoint partitions. Shared-subject and shared-stimulus projections need precise definitions.

The supplied algorithms are not implementable reliably: Algorithm 1 indexes an array of length N using stimulus indices up to M despite assuming M>N, and its loop direction conflicts with the prose saying one edge is selected per stimulus. Algorithm 2 contains analogous dimension/indexing problems, and splitting only by stories does not by itself guarantee disjoint subject sets. The proof that discarding samples is unavoidable also lacks necessary connectivity assumptions.

The advertised “fair benchmark” in Table 5 exactly matches the teacher-forced results in Table 6, although the paper itself reports substantially lower results without teacher forcing. A benchmark intended to measure generation from brain signals should use proper autoregressive inference as its primary result.

Comparisons are substantially confounded because the proposed method discards an unspecified amount of data. The paper reports neither retained sample counts nor effective train/validation/test sizes, and it does not explain the construction, size, or distribution of the additional test sets. Consequently, score differences cannot be cleanly attributed to leakage rather than training-set size or harder subjects/stories.

The encoder claim is unsupported: decreasing validation loss does not demonstrate degrading representations or overfitting, and no unseen-subject probe or external evaluation is provided. The predicted pattern is absent for EEG and is explained only speculatively.

Generation results lack uncertainty estimates or significance testing, despite random splitting and the use of “significant” language. Exact splits, performance seeds, shuffle granularity, decoding settings, and code are not released, preventing reproduction.

There is an internal contradiction: Tables 1–2 identify EEG method (d) as having text-stimulus leakage, whereas Appendix E calls it leakage-free and reports drastically different method-(d) scores in Table 8. The broad claim about “all current” approaches is also supported experimentally by only two models and one dataset per modality.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation confound in a relevant NLP/neurodecoding setting: repeated language stimuli can let powerful decoders exploit target regularities instead of brain signals.
The taxonomy of splitting strategies and the subject-story-text-signal graph provide a useful conceptual account of subject and stimulus overlap.

The evaluation spans fMRI and EEG, two datasets, and two established models. Additional holdouts, shuffled-input tests, longer training, and no-teacher-forcing experiments provide multiple diagnostic perspectives. The high scores that often persist after brain-input shuffling are a particularly valuable warning.
A jointly subject- and stimulus-disjoint benchmark could become a useful community resource, and the paper appropriately acknowledges that constructing it requires discarding observations.
weaknesses: The central framing is too categorical. Subject-disjoint evaluation with shared stimuli legitimately measures cross-subject transfer under controlled, previously seen stimuli; jointly holding out subjects and stimuli measures a harder, different generalization regime. Repeated targets create a shortcut risk, but are not definitionally train-test leakage. Consequently, claims that all existing splits are wrong or meaningless are not established by two models and two datasets.

The comparisons are not demonstrably fair. Splitting both axes 80/10/10 and retaining only matching blocks does not produce an 80/10/10 example-level split; in a fully crossed dataset it retains approximately 64%, 1%, and 1% of all examples for training, validation, and testing. The paper reports neither per-method sample counts nor discarded fractions and does not equalize training sizes or test composition, so score differences partly conflate leakage, data quantity, and test difficulty.

Important formal claims are incorrect or underspecified. Definitions 3.1-3.2 use a universal quantifier where existence of any overlapping pair is required; BSLR/TSLR invoke intersections of nominally disjoint sample sets without coherent conditioning; and the proof that discarding is always unavoidable assumes cross-story subject connectivity that was never stipulated. No proof or experiment shows that the proposed heuristic minimizes discarded data.

The evidence for causal claims is insufficiently controlled. The additional test sets are not defined with sizes, subjects, stories, or construction details; decoding scores lack multi-run uncertainty and significance testing; and shuffled inputs can retain sequence-length or other target-identifying cues without a length-matched or decoder-only baseline. Decreasing validation loss on a seen-subject validation distribution also does not demonstrate encoder overfitting or degraded unseen-subject representations.

The reported results contain serious inconsistencies. Tables 3-4 label several ROUGE values as F-scores although Tables 7-8 identify the same numbers as recall; Table 5 reports EEG2Text F=25.74 with R=23.98 and P=23.95; and method (d) for EEG is classified as stimulus-leaking in the main text but as leakage-free in Appendix E, with substantially different results. These errors directly affect the benchmark conclusions.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings. The pseudocode has swapped loop/index dimensions and cannot be implemented as written, exact preprocessing and split membership are delegated to prior papers, the added test construction is absent, and no code or released split files are provided despite the claim of releasing a benchmark. The core warning is promising, but corrected definitions, executable splits, controlled reruns, and substantially more transparent reporting are needed.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk in brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and repeated target stimuli can produce substantially different notions of generalization and may inflate apparent decoding quality.

The subject–story–text–signal perspective and taxonomy of common splitting strategies make the overlap mechanisms intuitive. A protocol holding out both subjects and stimuli is a useful strict benchmark for joint generalization.

The empirical investigation covers two modalities, two public datasets, and two established models. Additional-test-set, input-shuffling, longer-training, and no-teacher-forcing analyses provide converging, though not conclusive, evidence that repeated stimuli can encourage decoder memorization.

The manuscript is generally readable, includes implementation discussion and limitations, and reports markedly lower performance under its stricter split, which is a valuable warning for this research area.
weaknesses: The central claim that all existing splits are "wrong" and that the proposed split is uniquely "right" is not justified. Holding out subjects while retaining common stimuli is a legitimate protocol for measuring cross-subject transfer on controlled stimuli; holding out both axes measures a stricter joint subject-and-stimulus generalization problem. The paper should distinguish these estimands rather than label the former meaningless. Evidence from two models and datasets also cannot establish the claim about all current methods.

The formal analysis contains consequential errors. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification over training samples, whereas any leakage requires existence of at least one overlapping train/test pair. Equations 17–18 use ill-defined graph intersections and exact signal variables even though train and test samples are disjoint; as written, they cannot straightforwardly produce the reported nonzero rates. Moreover, the proposed rates largely reflect test/train count ratios rather than the fraction of test subjects or stimuli that overlap.

The splitting algorithms are not executable as written: loop variables, adjacency-matrix dimensions, and the lengths/indexing of C are inconsistent; three-way empty intersections do not establish pairwise disjointness; and the prose explicitly says variables should be altered inside omitted repetitions. For fMRI, selecting one subject per story does not guarantee disjoint subject sets unless additional matching or component constraints hold. The claimed general guarantee and proof that discarding samples is always unavoidable rely on unstated connectivity assumptions.

Crucial split statistics are absent: numbers of retained and discarded samples, subjects, stories, and text segments per partition are not reported. Consequently, comparisons among methods may be confounded by training-set size, test difficulty, and target distribution. Construction and size of the "additional test set" are also unspecified. Model results have no multi-seed uncertainty or significance analysis.

The headline results and the claimed fair benchmark reuse the "with teacher-forcing" values from Table 6. If, as the appendix states, teacher forcing is applied during generation, ground-truth prefixes directly contaminate evaluation. The free-running appendix does not repeat the key additional-test and shuffled-input controls. A language-only/no-brain baseline and a precise specification of what is shuffled are also needed.

A continuously decreasing contaminated validation loss does not demonstrate that encoder representations are degrading; it only shows improved loss on that validation distribution. The encoder-overfitting claim requires evaluation on an independent clean set of unseen subjects, preferably with a downstream probe or reconstruction metric.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings: no code, exact split assignments, or released benchmark artifact is provided, while preprocessing is delegated to prior papers and decoding details, metric implementations, and model-run seeds are missing. There are also internal reporting contradictions: the headline ROUGE1-F values correspond to the recall column in Tables 7–8, and Appendix E calls EEG method (d) leakage-free despite Table 2 reporting nonzero TSLR and other sections classifying it as leaky.

strengths: Targets an important evaluation problem: subject overlap and stimulus-text overlap can let powerful language decoders produce deceptively strong brain-to-text results.

The joint held-out-subject/held-out-stimulus split is sensible for evaluating generalization to both new people and new linguistic content, and the graph formulation highlights the dataset’s incidence structure.

The study triangulates evidence across fMRI and EEG, two datasets, two models, additional-test-set evaluation, shuffled brain inputs, longer training, and a teacher-forcing ablation. The broadly consistent direction of these results makes the leakage concern credible.
The manuscript clearly states its practical motivation and acknowledges important limitations, including discarded data and the weak contribution of existing brain encoders.
weaknesses: The central claim that all other splits are “wrong” is conceptually overstated. Holding out subjects while retaining shared stimuli is a legitimate evaluation of subject transfer for a fixed stimulus inventory; the proposed split instead measures joint subject-and-content generalization. These estimands should be distinguished, ideally through a seen/unseen subject × seen/unseen stimulus evaluation matrix.

Several core definitions are mathematically incorrect. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use a universal condition where the existence of any overlapping train/test pair would establish leakage. Equations 17–19 invoke the intersection of disjoint train and test sample sets, which is literally empty and does not encode subject or stimulus overlap. Consequently, the reported BSLR/TSLR values cannot be derived from the stated formulas.

The splitting pseudocode is not reproducible and conflicts with the method equations: loop indices and matrix dimensions are inconsistent, the EEG and fMRI expansion steps check only one partition axis and can reintroduce the other type of leakage, and triple-empty intersections do not establish pairwise disjointness. No executable code or fixed split files are provided despite the claimed benchmark release.

The empirical comparisons omit exact subject, story, and sample counts, discarded-data percentages, split identities, and training-set sizes. Because the proposed method both removes examples and creates a harder joint-generalization task, its lower scores cannot be attributed solely to eliminating leakage. Construction and matching of the “additional test set” are also unspecified.

The headline benchmark uses teacher-forced generation at evaluation—the main results match the “with teacher-forcing” column of Table 6. This is not a valid deployment evaluation for autoregressive decoding and confounds diagnostics such as shuffled-input performance. The non-teacher-forced setting appears only in one appendix table and is not used for the key additional-test and shuffled-input controls.

Some interpretations are unsupported: decreasing validation loss does not by itself demonstrate encoder overfitting or degraded representation, and increasing test performance with more epochs is not generally proof of leakage. An independent leakage-free encoder evaluation is needed.

Generation results lack uncertainty estimates or significance testing; only leakage-rate calculations use multiple seeds. This is especially problematic for ZuCo, which has only 12 subjects under an 80/10/10 split. Corrected definitions and algorithms, released partitions, matched-data comparisons, fully autoregressive evaluation, and repeated subject/story splits are needed before the work meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk: subject overlap and repeated target text are distinct axes, and repeated text can let an autoregressive decoder obtain impressive scores while relying little on neural input. This is highly relevant to brain-to-text NLP.

The empirical scope is useful: two signal modalities, two datasets, two representative models, several splitting strategies, and diagnostics involving a leakage-free auxiliary test set, shuffled brain signals, longer training, and teacher-forcing ablations.

The near-invariance to shuffled signals under text-overlapping splits, contrasted with larger degradation under the proposed split, is qualitatively compelling evidence that some published-style evaluations can reward target memorization.
The graph perspective could provide a useful basis for constructing subject-and-stimulus-disjoint benchmarks, and the paper candidly acknowledges data loss and weak encoder utilization.
weaknesses: The universal claim that all existing cross-subject splits are "wrong" is not justified. Subject-disjoint/content-seen, subject-seen/content-disjoint, and jointly unseen evaluations measure different generalization questions. Repeated targets are a serious confound for claiming open-ended decoding from brain activity, but are not automatically leakage for every explicitly defined transfer task. The paper needs a task taxonomy and a systematic audit of actual published protocols.

Several central definitions are mathematically incorrect. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal quantification where existence of any cross-split overlap is the relevant condition. Equations 17–20 place signals or texts in G_test intersect G_train; for disjoint sample sets these expressions are ill-typed or empty and cannot produce Table 2's nonzero values. Thus the proposed leakage metrics are not reproducible from their stated formulas.

The released pseudocode does not implement Equations 13–14: Algorithm 1 expands by subject without restricting text membership, while Algorithm 2 expands by story without restricting subject membership, potentially reintroducing the prohibited overlap. Loop orientations and matrix dimensions are also inconsistent, and a three-way empty intersection does not establish pairwise-disjoint partitions. The proof that samples must always be discarded is false for datasets with separable connected components.

No final split statistics are reported: numbers of subjects, stimuli, and samples per partition; identities of held-out stories/subjects; or the fraction discarded. Partitioning both axes 80/10/10 generally does not yield an 80/10/10 sample split and can make validation/test sets much smaller. Consequently, score differences may reflect training size, test size, or stimulus difficulty rather than leakage alone.

The claimed "fair benchmark" in Table 5 uses the teacher-forcing results; the corresponding free-generation results are substantially lower and appear only in the appendix. Gold-history decoding is unsuitable as the headline brain-to-text generation evaluation. The appendix also calls EEG method (d) leakage-free despite Section 3 and Table 2 saying it has text leakage, with results inconsistent with the main tables.

Key experimental details are missing, including how the additional test set is constructed and matched, exactly what is shuffled, decoding settings, retained dataset counts, and complete seeds. No code or concrete split files are provided. Referring to prior papers for filtering is insufficient given that splitting is the contribution.

Generation results appear to come from single runs/splits, without uncertainty, significance tests, or cross-subject folds. This is especially problematic for ZuCo's 12 subjects and content-dependent metrics. Comparisons also lack size-matched controls and a decoder-only or null-signal baseline.

A continually decreasing loss on a validation set containing training subjects does not demonstrate that the encoder is overfitting or that its representation quality is degrading; it only shows that this validation distribution is easier or non-independent. An independent held-out-subject evaluation is required, and the EEG experiment does not support the claimed encoder effect. These soundness and reproducibility problems preclude Findings in the current form, although a corrected implementation and controlled re-evaluation could plausibly support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk: when target passages recur across subjects, a powerful decoder can obtain impressive lexical-overlap scores without meaningfully using brain signals. This is highly relevant to brain-to-text NLP.
The study covers both fMRI and EEG, two datasets, and two established decoding architectures, rather than demonstrating the issue in only one setting.

The additional clean test set, shuffled-signal intervention, free-running decoding experiment, and longer-training analysis are useful complementary diagnostics. The large degradation under cleaner conditions provides credible qualitative evidence that published-style evaluations can substantially overestimate performance.
The subject–stimulus graph perspective is intuitive and points toward a useful practice: evaluations should explicitly state whether subjects, stimuli, or both are held out.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. Reusing stimuli or subjects is not intrinsically data leakage; it can define a legitimate transductive or within-subject estimand. Jointly holding out both is a demanding generalization regime, but not the uniquely “right” split. A factorial evaluation of seen/unseen subjects and seen/unseen stimuli is needed to distinguish these research questions.

The formal treatment contains serious errors. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal quantification where existence of any overlapping identity would define leakage. Equations 17–19 intersect disjoint train/test sample sets, which should produce an empty set rather than the reported rates, and the resulting BSLR/TSLR values are therefore neither well-defined nor reproducible from the formulas. The proof that discarding data is always unavoidable is also false without assumptions such as connectivity of the subject–stimulus graph.

The proposed algorithm is not implementable as written: loop indices and matrix dimensions conflict, `v.index`/`Minimum.index` are undefined, triple-set intersection does not establish pairwise disjointness, and the expansion pseudocode checks only one endpoint and can reintroduce the other type of leakage. The prose equations and algorithms also disagree, especially for fMRI.

Crucial split statistics are absent: retained and discarded sample counts, final numbers of subjects/stories/texts per partition, and exact split identities are not reported. Joint 80/10/10 partitioning can yield a very small test cross-product and markedly different training sizes, confounding comparisons with the other methods. This is particularly concerning for ZuCo's 12 subjects, where no subject-level cross-validation or multi-seed model evaluation is provided.

The construction, size, and difficulty matching of the “additional test set” are unspecified, so its lower scores could partly reflect content or distribution differences. Generation results have no uncertainty estimates or significance tests, and the encoder claim is inferred from validation-loss behavior that does not demonstrate degraded unseen-subject representations; the stated pattern also fails for EEG.

There are material internal inconsistencies. Method (d) is classified and measured as text-leaky in the main analysis, but Appendix E calls it leakage-free and Table 8 reports results incompatible with the main tables. strengths: The paper identifies a consequential evaluation confound: subject-disjoint splits can still expose the decoder to test stimuli, allowing apparent brain-to-text performance to reflect text memorization rather than neural decoding.

The separation of subject overlap from stimulus overlap is conceptually useful, and the graph-based formulation offers an intuitive basis for constructing splits that test both subject and language generalization.

The empirical case is triangulated across fMRI and EEG, two datasets, and two representative models. Results on an additional leakage-free test set and with shuffled brain inputs provide especially informative evidence that several reported scores are substantially inflated.
The topic is highly relevant to NLP evaluation and neuro-language modeling, and releasing reliable leakage-free splits could have considerable practical value for future work.
weaknesses: The paper overstates its central claim by calling one regime the universally "right" cross-subject split. Reusing stimuli is invalid for open-vocabulary generalization, but can be intentional when the estimand is transfer to new subjects under fixed stimuli. The paper should distinguish cross-subject, cross-stimulus, and joint generalization regimes rather than label all alternatives wrong.

Several formal definitions are incorrect or inconsistent with the experiments. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use a universal-existential condition rather than detecting any overlap, while Equations 17–20 appear to intersect disjoint sample sets and do not transparently yield Table 2. Consequently, BSLR and TSLR cannot be reproduced from the stated mathematics.

The appendix pseudocode contradicts the main equations. Algorithm 1 expands a split based only on subject membership, which can reintroduce test texts into training; Algorithm 2 checks only story membership, which can reintroduce test subjects. Loop directions, matrix dimensions, and the edge-selection description are also inconsistent. No executable implementation or released split indices are provided.

The paper does not report numbers of subjects, stories, text segments, or samples in each resulting partition, nor the fraction discarded. Because the proposed method can retain much less training and test data than the baselines, the claimed 8:1:1 comparison may not hold at the sample level and score differences are partly confounded by data quantity and distribution.

Key experimental details are missing, including construction and size of the additional test set, the precise shuffling procedure, generation settings, and training seeds. Model results are single point estimates without uncertainty or significance tests, and only two older systems are evaluated despite claims about all current methods.

Some interpretations are not justified: decreasing validation reconstruction loss under an easier subject-overlapping split does not demonstrate degrading representations, and test performance continuing to improve with training is not by itself evidence of leakage. The longer-training comparison also changes initialization and optimization settings simultaneously.

There are consequential internal inconsistencies: method (d) is alternately described as having and not having text leakage, and Appendix Table 8 appears to label leakage-free method (f) as method (d). Moreover, the advertised fair benchmark uses the teacher-forced scores even though Appendix E acknowledges that teacher forcing during generation materially inflates them. These soundness and reproducibility issues prevent a clear Findings recommendation, although they appear addressable in a substantial revision.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rlde8mf3/call-f9a6b34fcb3b4fa2b16ec09fd7cd783d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important evaluation problem: participant and target-stimulus overlap can let strong language decoders exploit memorization and substantially inflate apparent brain-to-text performance.

The study spans fMRI and EEG, two public datasets, and two established decoding architectures. The additional holdout, shuffled-input, longer-training, and teacher-forcing experiments are conceptually useful diagnostics.
Holding out both participants and stimuli defines a valuable, stringent joint-generalization benchmark. The motivating examples and graphical explanation make the high-level issue accessible.
weaknesses: The central assertion that all existing cross-subject splits are "wrong" conflates different evaluation objectives. A subject-held-out/shared-stimulus split can validly measure transfer to new participants for fixed content, whereas the proposed split measures the harder joint generalization to new participants and new content. Repeated targets create a memorization risk, but are not automatically leakage for every scientific question. The paper should distinguish these estimands and evaluate them factorially.

The formal definitions and leakage metrics are internally incorrect. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use a universal quantifier over training samples where existence of any cross-split overlap is relevant. Equations 17 and 18 use the intersection of disjoint train/test sample sets, which should be empty and does not express overlap after projection onto subjects or texts. Values near 12.5% for random splitting appear to reflect the test-to-training ratio; if every test subject is represented in training, the subject-overlap rate should instead be 100%. This undermines the central quantitative evidence.

The proposed algorithms are not reliably executable. Matrix and counter dimensions and loop indices are inconsistent; subject/stimulus disjointness is asserted without being enforced; and the expansion steps check only one endpoint, contrary to Equations 13–14. The proof that discarding samples is universally unavoidable also lacks necessary graph-connectivity assumptions. Exact split membership, realized sizes, and discarded-data fractions are not reported, so zero leakage and the claimed common 8:1:1 comparison cannot be verified.

The additional test set is not described in terms of construction, size, subjects, stories, or matching of difficulty. Performance differences therefore cannot be attributed causally to leakage, while similarity for method (f) may partly be a floor effect. Shuffling and non-teacher-forcing procedures are also underspecified, and a text-only or retrieval baseline is missing.

Most model results are single runs without uncertainty estimates or significance tests, which is particularly concerning for the 12-participant ZuCo dataset. The interpretation that continuously decreasing validation loss demonstrates encoder overfitting is not valid without training loss and evaluation on genuinely unseen subjects; the EEG result does not support that encoder claim.

There are consequential inconsistencies: ZuCo method (d) has nonzero TSLR and high scores in the main tables, yet the appendix calls it leakage-free and reports much lower, unchanged scores. No code, exact split files, or benchmark link is supplied despite the release claim, and preprocessing, model versions, generation settings, metric configuration, and training seeds remain incomplete. Correcting the formalism and implementation and rerunning the evaluation is necessary before the work meets Findings-level soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk for brain-to-text decoding: overlap in subjects and target stimuli can produce misleadingly optimistic results. This is highly relevant to NLP benchmarking. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-g1puogdc/call-2340fab03a9e4335bcb2ba7f119cea24/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The proposed subject-and-stimulus-disjoint perspective is useful, including the recognition that overlapping fMRI windows create an additional leakage route.

The experiments triangulate the issue across two modalities, two datasets, two models, additional held-out tests, shuffled-signal controls, longer training, and a no-teacher-forcing analysis. The large, consistent degradation on cleaner evaluations provides credible evidence that exact-stimulus overlap enables decoder memorization.
The manuscript is generally easy to follow, uses effective diagrams, acknowledges data loss from constrained splitting, and could motivate materially better evaluation practice.
weaknesses: The claim that all existing splits are "wrong" or "meaningless" conflates evaluation targets. A subject-disjoint but stimulus-shared split can validly measure transfer to new subjects conditional on controlled stimuli, whereas the proposed split measures harder joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli. The paper should distinguish these estimands and align conclusions with the claims each supports.

Several central definitions are mathematically inconsistent. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use a universal-over-training-samples condition rather than the existence of any cross-split overlap. In Equations 17-20, exact signal/text membership in the train-test intersection does not correctly express shared subject or stimulus identity and, for disjoint sample partitions, should be empty as written; the reported nonzero rates therefore cannot be reproduced from the formulas. The proof that discarding samples is always necessary also relies on unstated dataset-connectivity assumptions.

The splitting pseudocode is not executable as specified: loop directions, adjacency-matrix dimensions, and indices conflict with the prose, and asserted subject/stimulus disjointness does not follow transparently from the shown operations. No code, split files, subject/story identifiers, or discarded-sample counts are supplied, preventing verification of the claimed zero-leakage benchmark.

The proposed protocol simultaneously changes subject overlap, stimulus overlap, distribution, and training-set size. Without reporting entity/sample counts and matched-size controls, lower scores cannot be attributed solely to removing leakage. Model results also lack multi-seed uncertainty or significance analysis; this is consequential with only 12 ZuCo subjects and 27 Narratives stories.

The additional test set's construction, size, subjects, stories, and comparability are not documented, and the signal-shuffling procedure is unspecified. Moreover, decreasing loss on a contaminated validation set shows optimistic validation, not that encoder representations degrade on unseen subjects; a clean encoder evaluation and text-only/null-signal baselines are needed.

Table 5's purported fair benchmark reproduces the teacher-forced scores from Table 6. If gold prefixes are supplied during inference, these are not valid free-generation results. The no-teacher-forcing appendix usefully preserves the qualitative finding, but the benchmark and primary controls should use non-teacher-forced decoding throughout.

Coverage of two systems does not justify the repeated universal claims about "all current" methods, and the paper does not systematically map the five abstract split types to the surveyed literature. Overall, the insight is promising and the evidence is suggestive, but the formal errors, under-specified experiments, and invalid headline benchmark currently prevent the soundness and reproducibility required for Findings. Corrected definitions and algorithms, released splits, and controlled non-teacher-forced reruns could make a revised submission competitive.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-z6sy76n9/call-24cdbd5540254cb494693f7438e88412/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important evaluation problem: repeated subjects or exact stimuli across splits can substantially inflate apparent brain-to-text performance.
The subject-story-text-signal graph provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for distinguishing subject overlap from stimulus overlap and motivates evaluation on jointly unseen subjects and stimuli.

The empirical audit covers two modalities, two public datasets, and two established models. Additional-test-set, input-shuffling, longer-training, and no-teacher-forcing experiments consistently suggest that autoregressive decoders can exploit repeated targets while relying little on neural input.
The paper is generally readable, and its figures and tables make the central empirical pattern easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central normative claim is not established. Holding out subjects while retaining common stimuli is a legitimate protocol for measuring cross-subject transfer under controlled stimuli; it is not automatically data leakage. Jointly holding out subjects and stimuli measures a different and harder generalization regime. The paper should distinguish these scientific questions instead of declaring all alternatives "wrong" or "meaningless."

The formal foundation is internally incorrect. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification, requiring every training sample to overlap the test set, whereas leakage requires existence of at least one overlap. Equations 17-20 use intersections of train and test graphs that are otherwise defined as disjoint and do not operationalize subject identity consistently. Consequently, the reported BSLR/TSLR values cannot be derived from the written definitions.

The proposed algorithms are not executable as specified: adjacency-matrix dimensions and indices are inconsistent, and the expansion step in Algorithm 1 checks only subject membership while Algorithm 2 checks only story membership, contradicting Equations 13-16 and potentially reintroducing the other form of overlap. No code or exact split indices are provided.

The comparisons are strongly confounded by split composition. The proposed method discards cross-partition edges, but the paper never reports retained sample counts, numbers of subjects/stories/texts per set, or effective train/test ratios. Thus performance changes may reflect less training data and a harder distribution shift rather than leakage alone. The additional test set is also insufficiently described and is not shown to be size- or difficulty-matched.

The claimed "fair benchmark" in Table 5 uses the same teacher-forced results identified in Table 6, despite the paper acknowledging that teacher forcing during generation is problematic. The shuffled-input and additional-set analyses also appear to use this protocol. Free-generation shuffling and text-only/no-signal baselines are needed to substantiate the claim that predictions are independent of brain input.

The encoder evidence is misinterpreted: decreasing validation loss is not evidence that representation quality is degrading from overfitting. Demonstrating that claim requires training-versus-validation curves and evaluation on a genuinely subject-disjoint set or downstream probe; the EEG results in fact provide no supporting separation.

Generation results appear to be single runs without uncertainty or significance testing, while construction of random splits, BLEU/ROUGE aggregation, preprocessing details, and additional-test sampling remain underspecified. Together with the formal and algorithmic inconsistencies, this prevents the soundness and reproducibility required for Findings. The core audit is promising, but it needs reframing, corrected definitions and code, controlled no-teacher-forcing reruns, and complete split statistics before reconsideration.

strengths: The paper identifies a consequential evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding and usefully distinguishes subject overlap from target-text overlap.

The central empirical observation is supported from several angles across two public datasets and two representative systems: held-out non-overlapping tests, shuffled-signal controls, longer training, and an appendix experiment without teacher forcing. The large degradation when target texts are genuinely unseen is persuasive evidence that repeated stimuli can substantially inflate reported generation scores.

The proposed joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is a valuable evaluation setting, and the paper makes clear that existing systems derive limited benefit from their neural inputs under stricter evaluation.
The manuscript is relevant to NLP, generally readable, and provides some implementation settings and an appropriate ethics discussion.
weaknesses: The headline claim is overbroad. A held-out-subject split with shared stimuli legitimately measures cross-subject generalization conditional on known stimuli; it is not intrinsically data leakage. The proposed split instead measures the harder, distinct problem of joint subject-and-stimulus generalization. Evaluating two models and five selected split patterns also does not establish that all current methods are wrong or meaningless.

The formal account has substantive correctness problems. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use a universal condition where existence of any overlapping subject or text would define leakage. Equations 17–20 use intersections between disjoint train/test sample sets and mix graphs, samples, signals, and texts as though they were the same type. The proof that discarding data is always necessary is false for separable or disconnected subject–stimulus incidence graphs.

The pseudocode is inconsistent with the stated criterion and is not directly implementable: matrix dimensions and loop indices are mismatched, and the expansion step checks only subject membership for EEG or only story membership for fMRI, whereas Equations 13–14 require both dimensions to remain within the same partition. Pairwise separation among training, validation, and test partitions is also not specified correctly.

The proposed split discards data, but the paper never reports retained and discarded sample counts or per-partition numbers of subjects, stories, and text segments. Consequently, comparisons across splitting methods confound leakage with training-set size and test-set composition. The construction, size, and difficulty of the additional test sets are likewise unexplained.

The claimed fair benchmark in Table 5 reports the teacher-forced values reproduced in Table 6. Supplying gold prefixes during generation is not a valid open-ended decoding evaluation. Although the appendix shows that the leakage pattern persists without teacher forcing, the benchmark itself must be rerun and presented using genuine autoregressive inference.

The empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates or significance tests for generation results, despite stochastic training and ZuCo having only 12 subjects. The shuffling procedure is underspecified, and no decoder-only, constant-input, or language-model baseline is included. Moreover, decreasing validation loss on an overlapping validation distribution does not by itself demonstrate encoder overfitting or degraded representations.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: no code or fixed split files are provided, exact preprocessing and generation settings are incomplete, downstream random seeds are absent, and the erroneous pseudocode cannot recover the experimental partitions. These issues require substantial correction and rerunning before the contribution meets the Findings soundness and reproducibility threshold.

strengths: Identifies an important evaluation risk in brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and stimulus overlap are distinct generalization axes that should be reported explicitly.
The graph-based perspective and taxonomy of common splitting strategies are intuitive, and the distinction between overlapping fMRI windows and EEG samples is useful.

Experiments span two signal modalities, two datasets, and two established models. Additional-test-set, shuffled-input, teacher-forcing, and training-duration analyses provide several complementary warning signs that reported decoding scores can be inflated.
The topic is highly relevant to NLP evaluation and could materially improve future brain-to-text benchmarks if the protocol is corrected and released reproducibly.
weaknesses: The central claim that all existing cross-subject splits are "wrong" is not valid as stated. Holding out subjects while retaining shared stimuli is a legitimate protocol for measuring generalization to new subjects over a fixed stimulus inventory; the proposed method instead measures the stricter joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen texts. These estimands should be distinguished rather than labeling one universally correct.

Several formal definitions are incorrect or inconsistent. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use a forall-exists condition instead of detecting any overlap; Equations 17-20 use intersections whose meaning is incompatible with disjoint sample sets; and an empty three-way intersection does not establish pairwise-disjoint partitions. The claimed proof that discarding data is always necessary also fails without assumptions such as connectivity of the subject-stimulus graph.

The appendix algorithms are not executable descriptions of the proposed method: loop directions, array dimensions, and indices conflict with the prose, and the expansion steps do not enforce both subject and stimulus membership constraints. No code, fixed split files, or dataset-instance identifiers are provided, preventing reproduction of the benchmark.

Method (f) discards an unreported amount of data and can produce sample ratios very different from the claimed 8:1:1 ratio. The paper reports neither retained sample/subject/stimulus counts nor matched training budgets, so performance differences across splitting methods are confounded by dataset size, test difficulty, and composition. Construction and size of the "additional test set" are also unspecified.

The strongest shuffled-input evidence appears to use teacher-forced inference, itself an invalid generation evaluation. The non-teacher-forced study does not repeat the shuffled-input test or include text-only, zero-brain, unconditional-language-model, or retrieval baselines; consequently, higher scores under stimulus overlap do not by themselves prove paragraph memorization or that the task is meaningless.

The encoder analysis interprets continually decreasing validation loss as evidence of overfitting and degraded representations. That behavior only shows that a validation set with overlapping subjects is easier; degradation must be demonstrated on genuinely unseen subjects.

Results lack variance across model-training seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, and subject/story-level cross-validation. This is especially consequential for ZuCo, with only 12 subjects. There are also internal contradictions about whether EEG method (d) has text leakage. Addressing these issues requires corrected formalization, reproducible splits, and substantial experimental rerunning before the work is suitable for Findings.

In a crossed subject–stimulus design, partitioning both node sets can produce highly unequal example proportions and discard many cross-partition edges. There is also no optimization objective or evidence supporting the claim that the procedure minimizes discarded data. Consequently, score differences confound leakage, training-set size, test-set size, and distributional difficulty.

Several causal diagnostics are invalid or incomplete. Decreasing validation loss does not itself demonstrate encoder overfitting or degraded representations, and the EEG result does not support the claimed relationship. Likewise, continually improving test BLEU with more epochs is not diagnostic of leakage. These claims require matched held-out-subject probes, training curves, and controlled ablations.

The shuffled-input experiment appears to use teacher-forced generation, where ground-truth prefixes can themselves make the brain input largely irrelevant. Although Appendix E includes non-teacher-forced results, it does not combine that setting with the shuffled-input or additional-test controls. Moreover, the advertised "fair benchmark" in Table 5 reports the teacher-forced values, undermining that benchmark's validity.

Reproducibility and statistical support are inadequate: there is no code or split release, and the construction of the additional test set, unit of shuffling, decoding procedure, generation settings, split seeds, and post-filtering dataset sizes are unspecified. Performance is reported from apparently single runs without uncertainty or significance tests. Evidence from only two models and two datasets also cannot support the universal literature-wide claim. These issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation, though a carefully reframed and substantially corrected version could be ready for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important evaluation problem for brain-to-text decoding: repeated subjects and repeated linguistic stimuli can substantially inflate apparent generalization. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-geu3_6id/call-d2177e874d6a4683bf4e82e25b87a1cf/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical scope is useful: the study covers fMRI and EEG, two datasets, and two established architectures. Additional held-out tests, shuffled-signal controls, longer training, and the no-teacher-forcing appendix all point toward substantial score inflation when stimuli overlap.

Separating subject overlap from stimulus overlap is conceptually helpful. The graph presentation makes the dataset structure accessible, and a protocol jointly holding out subjects and stimuli could become a valuable benchmark.
weaknesses: The central claim that alternative cross-subject splits are categorically “wrong” is not justified. Cross-subject generalization requires unseen subjects, whereas unseen stimuli constitute a separate generalization axis. Testing new subjects on controlled, previously observed stimuli can be legitimate if that estimand is stated. The proposed protocol instead evaluates joint subject-and-stimulus generalization, and the paper should distinguish these settings rather than label all stimulus overlap as leakage.

Several formal definitions are incorrect. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use a universal quantifier over training samples although any overlapping pair would establish leakage. Equations 17–20 intersect G_train and G_test, which are disjoint sample sets, and mix signals/text vertices with graph samples; as written, these quantities cannot yield the reported nonzero rates. The claimed proof that discarding samples is always unavoidable is also false for datasets with separable connected components.

Algorithms 1–2 are not reliably implementable: loop directions conflict with the stated goal of selecting one edge per stimulus/story, adjacency dimensions and indices are inconsistent, and arrays sized for one vertex partition are indexed using the other. Splitting by tasks also does not by itself guarantee the asserted subject disjointness. No released code or exact split assignments compensate for these errors.

The comparisons do not report retained and discarded example counts, actual post-expansion split ratios, numbers of subjects/stories/texts per split, or the construction and size matching of the “additional test set.” Because method (f) changes training volume and imposes a harder distribution shift, its score differences cannot be attributed uniquely to leakage.

Generation results are mostly single runs without uncertainty or significance tests. This is particularly problematic for ZuCo, which has only 12 subjects; an 8:1:1 subject split leaves roughly one validation and one test subject. Subject-level cross-validation or multiple independently trained splits is needed.

The encoder analysis is logically insufficient: decreasing validation reconstruction loss is not evidence of overfitting or degraded representations. The shuffled-input experiment is informative but also lacks repeated shuffles and signal-free/constant-input language-model baselines, so it does not uniquely demonstrate memorization.

Table 5 uses the “with teacher-forcing” results even though Appendix E describes teacher forcing during generation and shows that it dramatically inflates scores. Unless this terminology is clarified, supplying ground-truth prefixes at evaluation invalidates the claimed fair benchmark; fully autoregressive results should be primary.

There is a direct internal contradiction: Tables 2–4 mark ZuCo method (d) as having stimulus leakage (TSLR 12.88%), while Sections 5.3 and Appendix E describe method (d) as leakage-free. This undermines the associated causal interpretation.

The underlying warning is promising, but correcting the definitions and algorithm, clarifying the evaluation estimand, rebuilding the benchmark without evaluation-time teacher forcing, reporting split statistics, and adding statistically robust controls are necessary before the work is sound and reproducible enough for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent cycle.

Holding stimuli fixed while testing unseen subjects is a legitimate controlled evaluation of subject transfer; the proposed split instead measures the harder joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli. These evaluation targets should be distinguished rather than declaring one uniquely correct.

The formalization contains consequential errors. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal rather than existential quantification; Equations 17–20 mix projected signals/text with intersections of sample graphs and do not transparently yield the reported rates; and the proof that samples must always be discarded is false without assumptions such as graph connectivity and nonempty partitions.

The published algorithms do not implement the stated criterion. Algorithm 1 expands a split while checking only subject membership, which can reintroduce held-out texts; Algorithm 2 checks only story membership, which can reintroduce held-out subjects. Their loop directions, matrix dimensions, and indexing are also inconsistent. Consequently, the reported zero-leakage results cannot be reproduced from the pseudocode.

The proposed method discards an unspecified amount of data, and an 8:1:1 split of seed vertices need not produce an 8:1:1 split of examples after expansion. The paper reports neither retained-example counts nor final per-split sizes, and does not explain construction or size matching of the additional test sets. Thus performance differences are confounded by training volume and test-set composition.

The main generation benchmark reproduces the paper's “with teacher-forcing” values, while Appendix E reports substantially lower results without teacher forcing and is ambiguous about whether gold prefixes are used at evaluation. Teacher-forced scores are not valid open-ended decoding results; free autoregressive generation should be the primary protocol, with a decoder-only or zero-brain baseline.

Most performance tables report one value without seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Moreover, decreasing validation loss is incorrectly treated as evidence that an encoder is overfitting and its representations are degrading; no held-out-subject probe supports that causal claim.

There are unresolved internal contradictions: EEG method (d) and fMRI method (e) are alternately described as leaky and non-leaky across the main text and Appendix E, with incompatible scores. Code, exact split manifests, preprocessing details, and complete randomization procedures are not provided despite the claimed benchmark release. These soundness and reproducibility problems preclude Findings in the current form, although the core diagnostic insight merits a revised submission.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-g911zumo/call-e9e4c00b67a8439f87bab5de3e406519/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} highlights an important NLP evaluation hazard: reusing subjects or exact target texts can allow a powerful decoder to exploit memorization rather than neural signals.
The graph formulation usefully separates subject generalization from stimulus generalization and could support better-designed brain-to-text benchmarks.
The study covers two signal modalities, two public datasets, and two established models. Additional holdouts, input shuffling, and a teacher-forcing ablation are valuable diagnostic ideas.
The large deterioration under stricter joint holdout conditions is a credible warning that prior headline scores may not measure open-ended decoding.
weaknesses: The central claim is conceptually overstated. Repeated stimuli are not intrinsically data leakage when the intended task is generalization to new subjects on a fixed stimulus set, just as repeated labels are legitimate in classification. The proposed split instead measures joint subject-and-stimulus generalization. The paper should define these distinct use cases and report a factorial benchmark rather than declaring every alternative split “wrong” or “meaningless.”

The formalization contains consequential errors. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 quantify over every training example rather than defining the existence of any overlapping subject or text; BSLR/TSLR use intersections of train and test graphs without coherently distinguishing samples, signals, and shared identities; and the proof that discarding data is unavoidable lacks necessary connectivity assumptions.

The pseudocode is inconsistent with the claimed zero-leakage construction and is not executable as written. Algorithm 1 expands a training subject with all of its text edges without excluding validation/test texts, while Algorithm 2 expands a training story without excluding validation/test subjects. Several loops also index arrays using incompatible subject/text dimensions.

Comparisons are confounded by uncontrolled data budgets. The proposed method discards an unreported fraction of examples, and an 8:1:1 partition of selected subjects/texts does not imply an 8:1:1 sample split. In a dense subject-by-text design, the construction would retain roughly 64% of all cells for training but only 1% each for validation and test. Exact split sizes, discarded fractions, identities, and distribution statistics are absent.

The primary benchmark is not a valid free-generation evaluation: its scores coincide with the appendix’s “with teacher-forcing” results, and the paper explicitly describes teacher forcing during generation. Supplying gold prefixes can make neural input largely irrelevant and directly confounds the shuffled-input diagnostic. Non-teacher-forced results are relegated to one ablation and are not used for the main benchmark or shuffle analysis.

Several empirical interpretations are invalid. Decreasing validation loss does not demonstrate overfitting, and improving test performance over more epochs does not prove leakage. The longer-training experiment simultaneously changes learning rate and encoder initialization. Likewise, comparing an original test set with an unspecified stricter “additional” test set changes subjects, stimuli, difficulty, and possibly size, so it does not isolate leakage causally.

Reproducibility and evidential rigor are inadequate for Findings: there is no released code or split manifest despite the claimed benchmark release; preprocessing is delegated to prior papers; additional-test and shuffling procedures are underspecified; retained sample counts are missing; and decoding results have no multi-seed uncertainty or significance testing. The potentially valuable warning therefore requires substantial reframing, corrected algorithms, and controlled reruns before publication.

weaknesses: The central claim is overgeneralized. Exact stimulus overlap is not automatically data leakage: holding stimuli fixed while holding subjects out is a legitimate design for isolating cross-subject generalization, just as repeated labels across splits are legitimate in supervised learning. The proposed split instead measures joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli. The paper should distinguish these estimands—ideally through a seen/unseen-subject × seen/unseen-stimulus evaluation—rather than call only one of them “right.”

Several formal definitions are incorrect. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use a universal quantifier over training samples when any overlap would require existential quantification. Equations 17–20 use intersections of nominally disjoint sample sets and mix signals/text elements with graph-valued sets, so they cannot straightforwardly produce the reported nonzero BSLR/TSLR values. The claimed universal proof that samples must be discarded also fails for datasets whose subject–stimulus graph has separable components.

The published pseudocode does not reliably implement Equations 13–16: loop variables and matrix dimensions appear transposed, the stated three-way intersections do not establish pairwise disjointness, and the expansion conditions check only one endpoint rather than both its subject and stimulus partition. No executable code, split files, or benchmark artifact is linked, making the proposed contribution inadequately reproducible.

Critical experimental details are absent: the construction, size, and composition of the “additional test set”; the axis and repetition count of signal shuffling; retained/discarded sample counts; resulting per-split subject/story counts; and model-run seeds. An 8:1:1 partition of graph representatives need not yield an 8:1:1 sample partition, and ZuCo has only 12 subjects. Single decoding scores without confidence intervals or subject-level variation cannot support broad claims.

The proposed split changes subjects, stimuli, training volume, and test difficulty simultaneously. Consequently, lower scores under method (f) do not by themselves quantify leakage. Matched-size controls, repeated graph partitions, and text-only/null-signal or stimulus-retrieval baselines are needed to isolate memorization from distribution shift and reduced data.

Table 5’s purportedly fair benchmark repeats the teacher-forced values, even though teacher-forced generation exposes ground-truth prefixes and is inappropriate as the principal free-generation benchmark. The appendix reports non-teacher-forced results, but does not combine that setting with the shuffled-input and additional-test controls.

The encoder conclusion is unsupported: decreasing validation reconstruction loss on a subject-overlapping validation set does not demonstrate that representations are degrading. Likewise, rising test performance with more training is not proof of leakage, and the corresponding experiment changes initialization, learning rate, and epoch count together. Appendix E also contradicts the main analysis by describing EEG method (d) as having no text leakage.

The underlying diagnostic is promising, but the conceptual conflation, erroneous formalization, under-specified split, and insufficiently controlled experiments prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation. These issues appear addressable through substantial reframing and rerunning within a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation issue in brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and stimulus-text overlap are distinct axes of generalization, and exact target-text overlap can substantially inflate generation metrics.
The graph-based taxonomy makes the alternative splitting regimes relatively easy to understand, and the proposed joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is a potentially useful stringent benchmark.

The evaluation spans two signal modalities, two public datasets, and two established models. Additional-test-set and shuffled-input diagnostics provide suggestive evidence that several reported systems rely heavily on target memorization or decoder priors.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. A held-out-subject split with shared stimuli legitimately measures transfer to new subjects on known stimuli; a held-out-stimulus split measures a different capability. The proposed method instead measures joint subject-and-stimulus generalization. These regimes should be distinguished in a factorial evaluation rather than declaring every existing split "wrong" or "meaningless."

Several formal definitions are incorrect or inconsistent with the prose. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification where any-overlap leakage requires existential quantification. Because training and test samples are disjoint, the intersections used in the BSLR/TSLR equations are also ill-defined or necessarily empty under the stated notation. Consequently, the reported rates cannot be reproduced from the formulas.

The splitting algorithm is not adequately validated. The pseudocode has inconsistent loop variables, adjacency-matrix dimensions, and balancing-array dimensions; it is unclear that it implements the mathematical construction. The proof that discarding samples is always unavoidable is false without additional assumptions on the incidence graph, and the claim of discarding as little data as possible has neither an optimization argument nor an empirical comparison.

Essential split statistics are missing: retained and discarded sample counts, subjects, stories and text segments per partition, and the resulting sample-level ratios. Joint partitioning can make validation and test sets far smaller than the stated 8:1:1 ratio and gives competing methods different training sizes and distributions, creating major confounds. This is especially concerning for ZuCo with only 12 subjects and no cross-validation or leave-one-subject-out aggregation.

The construction, size, composition, and relationship to model selection of the "additional test set" are not described. Thus, the large original-versus-additional performance differences do not isolate leakage from changes in subjects, stories, text difficulty, or dataset size.

The encoder conclusions are unsupported: decreasing validation loss is not evidence that representation ability is degrading, while increasing nonleaky validation loss is the conventional evidence of overfitting. No independent encoder evaluation on unseen subjects and stimuli is provided. Likewise, improving test performance with more training does not itself prove leakage, and Table 7 changes initialization, learning rate, and epoch count simultaneously.

There are material internal contradictions. EEG method (d) is described and measured as having text-stimulus leakage in the main analysis, but Appendix E calls it leakage-free and reports substantially different results. The role of teacher forcing at inference is also insufficiently specified, although it could directly affect the reported generation scores.

Model results appear to be single runs without uncertainty or significance testing; only leakage-rate calculations use multiple seeds. There is no released code or fixed split artifact cited, preprocessing is largely delegated to prior papers, and BLEU/ROUGE implementation details are absent. Text-only, constant-input, and repeated-shuffle baselines are also needed. These soundness and reproducibility gaps prevent a Findings recommendation, although the core evaluation question could support a substantially revised submission.

strengths: Identifies an important evaluation hazard in brain-to-text decoding: subject overlap and stimulus-text overlap are distinct, and jointly holding out both is necessary when the intended claim is generalization to new subjects and new language stimuli.

The decoder-side diagnostics are broad and mutually reinforcing. Results on two modalities, two datasets, and two models—especially the near-invariance to shuffled brain inputs under text overlap—provide compelling evidence that current systems can exploit target memorization.
The graph perspective makes the crossed subject–stimulus structure intuitive, and a reproducible joint held-out benchmark would be valuable to the NLP and cognitive-decoding communities.
The paper is generally well organized, and it includes seeds and several training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. A subject-disjoint, stimulus-overlapping split legitimately evaluates new-subject/seen-stimulus generalization; it is not inherently “wrong” or meaningless. The paper should distinguish the four subject/stimulus generalization regimes and restrict its conclusions to claims requiring joint generalization.

The formalization contains substantive errors. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal–existential conditions rather than defining leakage as the existence of any cross-partition overlap. Equations 17–20 use intersections of train and test sample sets that should be empty and do not coherently formalize identity overlap. The resulting BSLR is also tied to the split ratio—for example, approximately 12.5% despite essentially all test subjects being represented in training—rather than transparently measuring subject leakage.

The proposed algorithms are not reproducible as written: Algorithm 1 allocates C with subject length but indexes it by text, Algorithm 2 has the converse problem, loop directions conflict with the prose, and splitting one vertex set does not generally guarantee disjointness of the other. There is no proof that the greedy method achieves the requested balance or minimizes discarded data. The claimed inevitability of discarding samples is also false for arbitrary sparse graphs without additional connectivity assumptions.

Fairness of the empirical comparison is unresolved. The proposed method discards cross-block samples, yet the paper reports neither retained fractions nor final train/validation/test counts by subject, story, text segment, and sample. It does not demonstrate that the stated 8:1:1 ratio holds after expansion. Consequently, changes in training volume and test composition are confounded with leakage removal.

Crucial controls are under-specified: the construction, size, and matching of the additional test set; the precise shuffling operation; decoding settings; and the no-teacher-forcing procedure are not documented. Model scores lack variance or significance estimates, particularly problematic for ZuCo with only 12 subjects, and no code or fixed split artifacts are provided.

The claimed encoder damage is not established. A decreasing loss on a contaminated validation set does not show that representations are degrading, and the EEG curves do not support the proposed relationship. Likewise, monotonically improving test scores with more epochs is not a valid diagnostic of leakage, while some comparisons additionally change initialization and learning rate.

The main tables misreport ROUGE recall as ROUGE-1 F1. For example, Table 3 reports 40.65 for Narratives method (a), whereas Table 7 identifies 40.65 as recall and 44.83 as F1; the same column error propagates to the advertised benchmark. Corrected metrics and rechecked experiments are required.

The core warning is promising, but correcting the formal method, reframing the generalization claim, releasing executable splits, and rerunning matched, statistically supported evaluations constitute important revisions before the work is sound and reproducible enough for Findings.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation problem: subject overlap and repeated target stimuli can substantially inflate apparent brain-to-text performance.
The graph-based taxonomy makes several splitting protocols easy to compare, and the proposed split directly targets simultaneous subject and stimulus disjointness.

Experiments span fMRI and EEG, two datasets, and two established models. Additional-test-set, shuffled-input, longer-training, and no-teacher-forcing analyses provide useful converging evidence that some reported systems exploit target-text overlap and weakly use brain signals.
The negative result is relevant to NLP and could support a valuable standardized evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The central claim is overbroad. Stimulus overlap is not inherently leakage when the intended estimand is transfer to unseen subjects on known stimuli; the proposed protocol instead measures joint unseen-subject and unseen-stimulus generalization. These settings should be distinguished through a factorial evaluation rather than declaring all alternatives wrong or meaningless.

The formalization is unsound as written. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal rather than existential overlap conditions, while Equations 17–20 count intersections of disjoint train/test sample sets and contain indices that do not enter the summands. Consequently, the nonzero BSLR/TSLR values in Table 2 cannot be reproduced from the stated formulas.

The claimed proof that samples must always be discarded is false for datasets whose subject–stimulus graph already has separable components. The greedy algorithms also contain inconsistent loop directions and array dimensions and do not establish the asserted disjointness, target ratios, or minimal data loss.

Essential split statistics are missing: retained and discarded sample counts, subjects and stimuli per partition, effective ratios after expansion, and the construction and size of the additional test set. Since methods retain different data and induce different test distributions, score differences are not cleanly attributable to leakage.

Table 5 reproduces the “with teacher-forcing” results from Table 6. If, as the paper states, ground-truth previous tokens are supplied during generation, these are not valid free-generation benchmark scores; the no-teacher-forcing results should be primary.

There are material internal inconsistencies: EEG method (d) is marked stimulus-leaky in Tables 2–4, but Appendix E calls it leakage-free, and Table 8 reports substantially different method-(d) results. The claim that decreasing leaked-validation loss proves degraded encoder representations is also not justified without evaluation on an independent clean set.

Generation results lack uncertainty estimates or significance tests, and the blanket claim about all current methods is supported by only two models and two datasets. No executable code, fixed split assignments, complete decoding/metric details, or model-training seeds are provided, so reproducibility is insufficient for Findings. The core observation is promising, but the definitions, algorithms, benchmark, and controlled experiments require important revision.
