strengths: The manuscript identifies an important evaluation problem in repeated-stimulus neuro-language datasets and usefully distinguishes subject overlap from linguistic-stimulus overlap. This is directly relevant to reliable brain-to-text research in NLP. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-nyxe1jtt/call-eb6342a46de242bbbd37e7f41b0f5a83/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The intended subject-and-stimulus-disjoint benchmark is sensible for measuring joint generalization to unseen people and unseen linguistic content. The graph view also makes the underlying incidence constraints intuitive.

The audit spans fMRI and EEG, two public datasets, two representative decoding systems, and several common splitting strategies. The additional-test, shuffled-input, longer-training, and teacher-forcing diagnostics consistently suggest that reported generation scores can be dominated by linguistic memorization.
The paper is transparent about the large performance collapse under its stricter split and acknowledges data loss and excessive reliance on pretrained decoders.
weaknesses: The central claim is overgeneralized. Subject-disjoint/text-seen and subject-disjoint/text-unseen evaluation measure different legitimate estimands; repeated stimuli are leakage only when unseen-content generalization is claimed. The experiments therefore do not establish that all earlier cross-subject evaluations are intrinsically "wrong" or "meaningless."

Several formal statements are incorrect. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use a universal condition over every training sample instead of the existence of an overlapping train/test pair; Equation 9 is literally impossible when a sample is compared with itself; Equation 20 makes tau equal to one whenever its intersection is nonempty; and the proof that samples must always be discarded is false for, for example, a block-disconnected subject–stimulus graph.

The appendix pseudocode does not reliably implement Equations 13–14: loop variables and matrix dimensions are inconsistent, only triple rather than pairwise set intersections are constrained, and expansion checks only one endpoint, which can reintroduce overlap on the other endpoint. The fMRI construction likewise provides no general proof that selected subjects remain disjoint across story partitions.

The experimental comparisons are confounded by unreported data removal and split composition. The paper gives no retained/discarded sample counts or final subject, story, and text counts; thus the strict split may change training volume and test difficulty substantially. The construction and size of the "additional test set" are also unspecified.

Generation results are reported as single point estimates without training-seed variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The encoder conclusion relies only on validation-loss trajectories and does not demonstrate degraded representations on an independent clean set. Shuffling granularity and decoder-only or zero-signal controls are insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code URL, executable splitting implementation, or released split manifest to resolve the pseudocode errors. Reporting is also internally inconsistent—for example, method (d) is characterized differently across sections, and values labeled ROUGE-1 F in Tables 3, 4, and 6 align with the recall column in Tables 7–8. These issues prevent a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation, although the core audit appears repairable for a next-cycle submission.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk: reusing exact target passages across subjects can let an autoregressive decoder exploit linguistic memorization rather than demonstrate open-vocabulary brain-to-text decoding.
Separating subject overlap from stimulus overlap is conceptually useful, and the graph-based taxonomy makes several common splitting protocols easier to compare.

The evaluation spans two signal modalities, two datasets, and two established models. Additional held-out tests, shuffled-brain inputs, longer training, and a no-teacher-forcing ablation all provide qualitatively useful diagnostics.
The large performance reductions under stricter splits are practically consequential and should prompt the community to state clearly whether it evaluates unseen subjects, unseen stimuli, or both.
weaknesses: The central claim that all other cross-subject splits are "wrong" is not valid without specifying the intended estimand. A held-out-subject/seen-stimulus protocol legitimately measures cross-subject transfer, whereas the proposed protocol measures the harder joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli. These should be presented as distinct tasks, not as leakage versus correctness.

The formalization contains serious errors. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification where existence of any overlapping subject or stimulus would define leakage. Equations 17–20 use ill-typed intersections between signals/texts and graphs; if train and test are disjoint sample sets, their literal intersection is empty. Consequently, BSLR and TSLR do not transparently measure the properties claimed.

The proposed algorithms are not reproducible as written: matrix dimensions, loop variables, and indices conflict with the stated node sets, and the fMRI procedure does not clearly guarantee simultaneous subject and story disjointness. The proof that samples must always be discarded is also false for datasets whose subject–stimulus graph already has separable components.

The paper never reports final train/validation/test sample counts or the amount discarded. Expanding only within matched subject–stimulus partitions generally changes the nominal 80/10/10 proportions substantially. Comparisons therefore confound leakage with training-set size, test composition, and distribution shift; matched-size controls are needed.

Construction and sample sizes of the "additional test set" are unspecified. Model results appear to come from single splits, with no subject/story-level cross-validation, uncertainty estimates, or significance testing. This is especially concerning for ZuCo, which has only 12 subjects.

The advertised fair benchmark uses the teacher-forcing numbers reproduced in Table 6. If gold prefixes are supplied during test-time generation, this is not a valid free-generation benchmark and also confounds the shuffled-input evidence. The no-teacher-forcing results should be primary and should include decoder-only or no-brain baselines.

There are consequential internal inconsistencies: method (d) is described both as having and not having text leakage, and its ZuCo results differ drastically between Tables 4 and 8 under ostensibly comparable settings. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the experimental record.

No code, realized split files, retained-data statistics, or sufficiently complete preprocessing and decoding specifications are provided. Combined with the erroneous pseudocode, this falls short of Findings-level reproducibility.

The underlying warning is valuable, but the task framing, split construction, formal definitions, and controlled evaluation require important revision and rerunning before the central claims and benchmark can be accepted.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6rcbvs20/call-c373691d2a53402ca5da4f9bfb469b62/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important evaluation problem: subject overlap and stimulus overlap can let brain-to-text systems obtain impressive scores without demonstrating generalization to unseen people and language.

The empirical results contain valuable warning signs. Performance collapses on the additional zero-overlap test set, while shuffled brain inputs often barely affect nominally strong systems, suggesting that reported scores can be dominated by the decoder or stimulus memorization.

The study covers both fMRI and EEG, two public datasets, and two representative encoder-decoder models. The additional-test, input-shuffling, longer-training, and non-teacher-forced experiments are useful diagnostic directions.
The distinction between subject and stimulus overlap is intuitive and relevant to future benchmark design.
weaknesses: The central framing is too categorical. Subject or stimulus overlap is not automatically data leakage; these choices define different legitimate generalization settings. A subject-disjoint, stimulus-seen test can assess closed-set transfer to new subjects. The proposed split instead tests joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli. The paper should present an orthogonal 2-by-2 evaluation and align claims with each setting rather than declaring one universally “right.”

The formalization and pseudocode contain correctness problems. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal rather than existential overlap conditions, the BSLR/TSLR intersections are not well-defined under the graph construction, and the proof that discarding data is unavoidable lacks required connectivity assumptions. More seriously, Algorithm 1 expands a partition based only on subject membership, and Algorithm 2 based only on story membership, so the written algorithms can reintroduce overlap at the other endpoint. Their indexing and array dimensions are also inconsistent.

The headline benchmark and most diagnostic tables use teacher forcing during test-time generation. Supplying ground-truth prefixes is itself target information and invalidates the benchmark as an assessment of autonomous brain-to-text generation. Non-teacher-forced scores appear only in an appendix, without the full shuffled-input and additional-test controls.

The comparisons confound overlap with substantial distribution and sample-size changes. The proposed method discards an unreported amount of data and simultaneously changes subjects and stimuli. The additional test set is not described in terms of construction, size, matching, or composition, so its score gap cannot be attributed solely to leakage.

Statistical support is inadequate. Variability is reported only for leakage-rate calculations, not decoding results; there are no confidence intervals or significance tests despite claims of significant differences. This is especially problematic for ZuCo, which has only 12 subjects.

The encoder conclusion is unsupported: decreasing validation loss on overlapping subjects shows that the validation distribution is easier, not that representation quality is degrading. No genuinely held-out-subject probe is provided, and the EEG experiment does not reproduce the claimed pattern.

Reproducibility is insufficient for Findings. The paper provides no executable code, fixed split identifiers, post-filtering sample counts, retained/discarded proportions, model-run seeds, or adequate generation, tokenization, checkpoint-selection, and metric details. There is also an internal contradiction over whether EEG method (d) has stimulus leakage.

The broad claims about all current methods and a fair SOTA benchmark are supported by only two older architectures. Stronger evidence would include newer systems plus text-only, no-brain, and retrieval baselines evaluated autoregressively. The underlying concern is important, but these soundness and reproducibility problems require a substantial revision and rerun before publication.

strengths: The manuscript raises an important evaluation issue for brain-to-text research: target-text reuse across subjects can substantially inflate apparent decoding performance. This is highly relevant to NLP and neurotechnology. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-ophmx81h/call-66a208910ec445a39be9417a89570111/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The taxonomy of subject-, story-, and signal-based splits, together with the graphical exposition, makes the different overlap patterns relatively accessible.

The additional-holdout and shuffled-input experiments span fMRI, EEG, two datasets, and two model families. Their qualitative pattern provides useful evidence that some previously reported scores reflect target overlap or decoder behavior more than information extracted from brain signals.
weaknesses: The central claim conflates different evaluation targets. Reusing a subject is not automatically data leakage when evaluating generalization to new stimuli for known subjects; likewise, reusing stimuli can be legitimate when evaluating transfer to unseen subjects under a fixed stimulus set. The proposed split instead tests the harder double-cold-start setting of unseen subjects and unseen texts. That is valuable, but it does not make every alternative split “wrong” or “meaningless.”

The formal definitions are incorrect as written. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use a universal-over-training-samples condition rather than the existential condition needed to detect any overlap. Equations 17–18 intersect nominally disjoint train and test sample sets, so the BSLR numerator for exact brain-signal objects should be zero; this does not match the reported nonzero values. Consequently, the leakage metrics cannot be reproduced from their mathematical definitions.

The proposed algorithms do not reliably implement the stated criterion. Algorithms 1–2 contain reversed matrix dimensions and indices, disagree with the main text about which vertex set is selected and split, and their expansion steps constrain only one endpoint, potentially reintroducing stimulus or subject overlap. The proof that discarding samples is always necessary is also false without assumptions such as connectedness of the subject–stimulus incidence graph.

Comparisons across splitting methods are confounded. The paper does not report subjects, stories, text segments, or examples per split; the fraction discarded; or the resulting ratios after expansion. The claimed 8:1:1 vertex split does not generally produce an 8:1:1 sample split, so performance differences may partly reflect unequal training sizes and test distributions.

The “additional test set” is insufficiently specified: its construction, size, subject/story composition, and relationship to model selection are absent. Model results are single runs without uncertainty or significance testing, while only the mechanically computed leakage rates use multiple seeds.

The main tables and the proposed “fair benchmark” appear to use teacher-forced decoding. Table 6 shows that removing teacher forcing dramatically changes the results, yet the paper does not repeat its shuffled-input or additional-test controls under free-running generation. A language-only/no-brain baseline is also missing, so decoder memorization is not cleanly isolated.

The encoder conclusion is unsupported: decreasing validation reconstruction loss on overlapping subjects does not demonstrate that representation quality is degrading. The EEG experiment yields no predicted distinction, and increasing test performance over additional epochs is neither proof of leakage nor an appropriate substitute for validation-based model selection.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or fixed splits are linked, and essential filtering counts, preprocessing details, shuffle procedure, checkpoint selection, tokenization, BLEU smoothing, and random seeds are missing. There are also internal contradictions, including describing EEG method (d) as leakage-free in Appendix E despite reporting nonzero TSLR elsewhere. Correcting the definitions and executable split, then rerunning controlled free-generation experiments, is necessary before Findings-level soundness can be established.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation risk in brain-to-text research: repeated target passages can let a powerful decoder obtain high overlap scores without relying strongly on brain signals. This is highly relevant to NLP evaluation. Reviewed manuscript: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gi8abzuz/call-570a9d419cd0442b9a60dd931eb10e67/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation covers fMRI and EEG, two public datasets, and two established encoder-decoder systems. Additional held-out evaluation, input shuffling, and training-length analyses all provide useful diagnostic perspectives.
The distinction between subject overlap and stimulus overlap is potentially valuable, and the graph-based presentation makes the dataset structure intuitive.

The large score reductions under stricter evaluation provide credible evidence for the narrower conclusion that previously reported scores may substantially overstate joint generalization to unseen subjects and unseen stimuli.
weaknesses: The central claim that every alternative split is "wrong" conflates leakage with the intended generalization setting. Unseen-subject/seen-stimulus, seen-subject/unseen-stimulus, and jointly unseen evaluation answer different legitimate questions. The proposed split is appropriate for the third setting, but it is not uniquely correct for all cross-subject research.

The formal definitions are internally invalid. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal-existential quantifiers that require every training sample to have a test counterpart, whereas the prose treats any overlap as leakage. Equations 17–20 contain unbound or mismatched indices, and the literal intersection of disjoint sample sets cannot yield the reported nonzero brain-signal leakage rates. Thus the theoretical characterization and novel metrics are not reproducible as written.

The proposed algorithms do not faithfully implement the stated criterion. Algorithm 1 has dimension/index inconsistencies, while its expansion condition restricts subjects but not text nodes; Algorithm 2 analogously restricts stories but not subjects. Either expansion can reintroduce the overlap the method is meant to eliminate. No executable implementation or released split is provided.

The method discards data, but the paper reports neither split cardinalities nor discard rates, subject/story distributions, or training-set sizes. There is no proof that the heuristic minimizes discarded data. Consequently, performance differences for method (f) are confounded by data quantity and composition rather than isolating leakage.

The additional test sets are not described in terms of construction, size, subjects, stories, or difficulty. Comparing their scores with the original test sets therefore does not establish a causal leakage effect. Downstream results also lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and sample-matched controls.

The encoder conclusion is unsupported: steadily decreasing validation loss on seen subjects is not evidence that representation quality is degrading or that the encoder is overfitting. An unseen-subject reconstruction or probing evaluation is needed, and the EEG experiment supplies no corroborating evidence.

The advertised "fair benchmark" uses teacher-forced generation: its values match the teacher-forced side of Table 6, even though the appendix shows that removing teacher forcing causes large reductions. Feeding test-reference prefixes during generation is itself target information, so all principal diagnostics and benchmark results should be rerun with standard free-running decoding and text-only or unconditional baselines.

There are material internal inconsistencies. For example, ZuCo method (d) has nonzero text overlap and is treated as leaking in Tables 2–4, but Appendix E calls it leakage-free; its Table 8 scores also differ radically from the earlier method-(d) results. Preprocessing, shuffling granularity, tokenization, decoding settings, checkpoint selection, and model-training seeds are insufficiently specified.

The narrow evaluation of two systems and two datasets cannot support claims about "all current" methods, and the closest prior critical audit, Jo et al. (2024), is not adequately positioned. The useful empirical warning is salvageable, but the split, formal analysis, and benchmark require substantial correction and controlled rerunning before the work is sound and reproducible enough for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a next-cycle resubmission.

strengths: Identifies an important evaluation risk: subject-disjoint and stimulus-disjoint evaluation measure different generalization abilities, and ignoring either axis can substantially inflate apparent brain-to-text performance.
The graph-based framing clearly exposes the subject–stimulus structure of naturalistic neuroimaging datasets.

Evaluation spans two architectures, two signal modalities, and several useful diagnostics, including an additional holdout set and shuffled brain inputs. The large score collapses provide credible evidence that some published protocols permit substantial linguistic memorization.
The topic is highly relevant to NLP benchmarking and could support a valuable Findings contribution after correction and stronger validation.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated: repeated stimuli across subjects are not universally “data leakage.” A subject-disjoint, same-stimulus split can validly measure generalization to new subjects, while joint subject-and-stimulus holdout measures a harder, different estimand. The paper should distinguish these regimes instead of declaring all existing splits wrong.

The formalization is internally invalid. Equations 6–7 use universal quantification where existence of any overlap is intended, while Equations 17–20 invoke intersections of nominally disjoint train/test sample sets and therefore cannot yield the reported nonzero leakage rates as written.

Algorithms 1–2 are dimensionally inconsistent and their expansion conditions omit one disjointness axis, contradicting Equations 13–14 and potentially reintroducing leakage. No executable code or exact split files are supplied to resolve the ambiguity.

The empirical comparisons confound leakage with dataset composition and difficulty. The proposed split discards an unreported amount of data, and the “additional test set” construction, size, subjects, and stimuli are unspecified. Consequently, score differences do not isolate the causal effect of leakage.

There are serious result inconsistencies: ZuCo method (d) is treated as text-leaky in the main tables but described as leakage-free in Appendix E, where its nominal 50-epoch results also differ dramatically from Table 3.

The encoder conclusion is unsupported: decreasing validation loss under overlapping subjects does not demonstrate deteriorating representations or overfitting. Evaluation on genuinely unseen subjects, with training curves and an independent representation metric, is needed.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a proposed benchmark: retained/discarded sample counts, exact partitions, preprocessing details, shuffling procedure, teacher-forcing protocol, decoding/tokenization settings, uncertainty for model results, and significance tests are missing.

The benchmark relies only on BLEU/ROUGE and lacks text-only, retrieval, or decoder-prior baselines. Together with single-run generation results, this limits evidence that the leakage-free scores reflect information decoded from brain signals.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation-validity problem for brain-to-text decoding: repeated target text across subjects can let a powerful decoder memorize language rather than use neural signals. This is highly relevant to NLP and cognitive decoding.

The proposed joint subject-and-stimulus holdout targets the practically meaningful setting of generalization to both unseen people and unseen content. The graph-based illustrations make the possible overlap patterns intuitive.

Evidence comes from two modalities, two public datasets, and two representative models. The additional held-out test sets, shuffled-input controls, longer-training experiments, and non-teacher-forced ablation consistently suggest substantial score inflation when target text is repeated.
The large performance differences are practically consequential, and establishing leakage-resistant benchmark splits could be a valuable community contribution.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated. Sharing a subject or stimulus across splits is not inherently data leakage; it defines a different estimand, such as unseen-sample, unseen-subject, or unseen-stimulus generalization. The paper should motivate its deployment target and evaluate the full seen/unseen-subject by seen/unseen-stimulus matrix. The present joint holdout changes both axes simultaneously and does not justify declaring all other protocols wrong.

Several formal definitions are incorrect. Definitions 3.1 and 3.2 use universal quantification where an existential overlap would establish leakage. Equations 17–20 intersect the training and test sample sets, which should be disjoint under any ordinary split and therefore cannot yield the reported nonzero rates. The appendix claim that samples must always be discarded also relies on unstated connectivity assumptions and is not generally true.

The supplied algorithms are not reproducible as written. Algorithm 1 has incompatible array dimensions and loop/index roles, while Algorithm 2 splits by stories and then merely asserts, without enforcing, disjoint subject sets. No executable implementation or released split assignments are provided.

The experiments omit essential split statistics: retained and discarded sample counts, numbers of subjects/stories/text segments per partition, and the exact construction and size of the additional test set. Because the proposed method discards data, its lower results are confounded with changes in training size and distribution. Generation results also lack repeated-run uncertainty or significance analysis.

There are serious internal result inconsistencies. For ZuCo, method (d) has nonzero TSLR and high leaky-split scores in Tables 2–4, but Appendix E calls it leakage-free and Table 8 reports radically different scores. Method (e) is visually labeled leakage-free despite nonzero TSLR. Several values labeled ROUGE-1 F in Table 3 correspond to the recall column of Tables 7–8, and some precision/recall/F triples in Table 5 are mathematically incompatible.

The advertised fair benchmark appears to use teacher forcing during test generation: its scores match the teacher-forced side of Table 6. Supplying gold target prefixes makes this unsuitable as the primary brain-to-text benchmark; free-running results should be primary and accompanied by a language-only baseline.

The claimed damage from subject overlap to the encoder is not established. A decreasing validation reconstruction loss on seen subjects is not evidence that representation quality is degrading. An independent unseen-subject evaluation or downstream probe is needed.

Overall, the repeated-text diagnosis is promising, but the mathematical errors, contradictory tables, confounded comparisons, and missing reproducibility artifacts prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form. Correcting the protocol and rerunning the analyses appears feasible for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a consequential evaluation-validity problem in brain-to-text decoding. Distinguishing subject overlap from repeated-stimulus/target overlap is useful and highly relevant to NLP and neuro-language modeling.

The empirical diagnostics span two modalities, two public datasets, and two architectures. Clean-test comparisons, shuffled brain inputs, longer-training checks, and teacher-forcing ablations collectively provide credible evidence that some published scores can be dominated by language-side shortcuts rather than brain signals.

The graph-based formulation clearly exposes the coupled subject–stimulus structure of naturalistic datasets and motivates jointly subject- and stimulus-disjoint evaluation. The figures communicate the intuition effectively, and the limitations are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: The central claim is conceptually overstated. A subject-held-out, seen-stimulus split can legitimately evaluate transfer to new subjects under a closed stimulus set; the proposed split instead evaluates simultaneous new-subject and new-stimulus generalization. These are different estimands, not simply “wrong” versus “right” splitting. A two-by-two evaluation of seen/unseen subjects and stimuli is needed.

The formalization contains substantive errors. Definitions 3.1–3.2 use universal quantification where the existence of any overlap would define leakage; Equations 17–20 use intersections of nominally disjoint sample graphs and do not operationalize the prose definitions clearly; and the claimed proof that discarding samples is unavoidable is false without additional connectivity assumptions.

Algorithms 1–2 are not reproducible as written: matrix dimensions conflict with indexing, loops select along the wrong graph side, and the expansion conditions check only the subject endpoint for EEG or the story endpoint for fMRI, potentially reintroducing overlap on the other endpoint. The fMRI description also changes the selection unit across sections, and no executable code or exact split files are provided.

The additional test set is never adequately defined. The paper omits post-filtering sample counts, subjects/stories per split, retained and discarded fractions, and achieved sample ratios. The greedy construction is neither proven nor empirically shown to minimize discarded data or distribution imbalance. Consequently, comparisons across splitting methods confound leakage with training-set size and test-set difficulty.

The causal controls remain incomplete. Table 4’s shuffled-input results use the same scores identified as teacher-forced in Table 6, but the crucial shuffled-input-by-free-generation experiment is absent. Moreover, the purported fair benchmark in Table 5 reports teacher-forced scores despite demonstrating that this evaluation inflates results. Increasing test performance over epochs is also not, by itself, evidence of train–test leakage.

There are serious reporting inconsistencies: Section 3.2 and Table 2 classify EEG method (d) as having stimulus leakage, whereas Appendix E calls it leakage-free; Table 8’s method-(d) values conflict sharply with the corresponding 50-epoch results in the main tables and may actually be mislabeled method-(f) results.

Generation results lack multi-seed uncertainty, statistical tests, and subject-fold evaluation, which is particularly concerning for ZuCo with only 12 participants. Testing only two 2022–2023 models also does not substantiate claims about “all current” methods or establish a sufficiently broad benchmark. These soundness and reproducibility issues require corrected formalism, released splits/code, and controlled reruns before Findings publication is warranted.
